stem: The chapter shows that a rectangle can be defined using only one condition. Which condition is enough to define a rectangle?
options: Both pairs of opposite sides of the quadrilateral are parallel
All four angles of the quadrilateral are right angles
The two diagonals of the quadrilateral bisect each other
The two diagonals of the quadrilateral are perpendicular
explanation: Correct option: (B). The chapter proves (Deduction 4) that if all the angles of a quadrilateral are 90 degrees, its opposite sides are automatically equal, so a rectangle can be defined simply as a quadrilateral with all angles 90 degrees. Parallel opposite sides or bisecting diagonals describe every parallelogram, and perpendicular diagonals describe rhombuses and kites, so none of these alone gives a rectangle.

stem: A carpenter has one wooden strip 8 cm long and wants the endpoints of two strips to be the corners of a rectangle. How must the second strip be chosen and placed?
options: It must be 4 cm long and joined at the midpoint of the first strip
It must be 8 cm long and joined at right angles to an end of the first
It must be 8 cm long and the strips joined at their midpoints
It may be of any length if the strips are joined at right angles
explanation: Correct option: (C). The strips are the diagonals of the quadrilateral. A quadrilateral whose diagonals are equal and bisect each other is a rectangle, so the second strip must also be 8 cm and the strips must cross at their midpoints, at any angle. A 4 cm strip gives unequal diagonals, joining at an end means the diagonals do not bisect each other, and the right angle is not needed (it would give a square only with equal diagonals).

stem: In rectangle ABCD, the diagonals AC and BD meet at O. If AC = 10 cm and angle AOB = 50 degrees, what is the measure of angle OAB?
options: 50 degrees
130 degrees
25 degrees
65 degrees
explanation: Correct option: (D). The diagonals of a rectangle are equal and bisect each other, so OA = OB = 5 cm and triangle AOB is isosceles. Its base angles are equal: 2 x angle OAB + 50 = 180, so angle OAB = 130/2 = 65 degrees. 50 degrees copies the angle at O, 130 degrees is the angle AOD (the linear pair), and 25 degrees halves 50 instead of halving 180 - 50.

stem: Riya constructs 20 different rectangles and finds by measuring that the diagonals of each one bisect each other. What is the best description of her result?
options: A conjecture, which becomes certain only when it is proved
A proof, because 20 different cases are enough to be fully certain
A false claim, because measurements always contain small errors
A definition of a rectangle, so it does not need to be proved
explanation: Correct option: (A). Observations from measurement give useful insight but only a conjecture: we cannot be sure the next (say the 1000th) rectangle behaves the same way. The chapter proves the property using congruent triangles (Deduction 2). Any number of examples is not a proof, measurement error does not make the statement false, and the property is a deduced result, not the definition.

stem: Two equal diagonals AC and BD bisect each other at O, and angle AOB = x. Since OA = OD, triangle AOD is isosceles. Which expression gives the base angle OAD?
options: 90 - x/2 degrees
x/2 degrees
180 - x degrees
90 - x degrees
explanation: Correct option: (B). Angle AOD and angle AOB form a linear pair, so angle AOD = 180 - x. In isosceles triangle AOD, 2b + (180 - x) = 180, so 2b = x and b = x/2. The expression 90 - x/2 is the base angle of triangle AOB, not AOD; 180 - x is the angle at O itself; 90 - x comes from wrongly using x in place of x/2. Adding the two base angles at A gives (90 - x/2) + x/2 = 90 degrees, which is why the figure is always a rectangle.

stem: Which statement correctly describes the relation between squares and rectangles?
options: Every rectangle is a square, but not every square is a rectangle
A square is never a rectangle because all its sides are equal
Every square is a rectangle, but not every rectangle is a square
Squares and rectangles are exactly the same set of shapes
explanation: Correct option: (C). A square has all angles 90 degrees, so it satisfies the definition of a rectangle; it is a special rectangle whose sides are also all equal. A rectangle with sides 6 cm and 2 cm is not a square, so the reverse is false. In a Venn diagram, the set of squares lies inside the set of rectangles, which rules out the other three statements.

stem: In a circle with centre O, PL and AM are two diameters that are perpendicular to each other. What type of quadrilateral is APML?
options: A rectangle that is not a square
A rhombus that is not a square
A square
A kite that is not a rhombus
explanation: Correct option: (C). The diagonals of APML are the diameters PL and AM. They are equal (each is twice the radius), they bisect each other at the centre O, and they are perpendicular. A quadrilateral whose diagonals are equal and bisect each other at right angles is a square. Equal bisecting diagonals alone would give a rectangle, but the right angle makes it a square; a rhombus that is not a square has unequal diagonals, and a kite's diagonals need not bisect each other.

stem: CASE is a square, and U, V, W and X are the midpoints of its sides, taken in order. Which conclusion about UVWX is correct?
options: It is a square, since its sides are equal and each angle is 90 degrees
It is a rectangle that is not a square, since only its angles are 90 degrees
It is a rhombus that is not a square, since only its sides are equal
It is a kite that is not a rhombus, since its diagonals are perpendicular
explanation: Correct option: (A). Each corner triangle, such as CUV, is right-angled with equal legs (half the side of the square), so the four triangles are congruent and UV = VW = WX = XU. Each corner triangle is isosceles with base angles of 45 degrees, so at each vertex of UVWX the angle is 180 - 45 - 45 = 90 degrees. Equal sides and right angles make UVWX a square, so the claims that only the sides or only the angles qualify are wrong, and a kite that is not a rhombus cannot have four equal sides.

options: 180 degrees
360 degrees
540 degrees
720 degrees

stem: In quadrilateral SOME, the diagonal SM is drawn. Why does this show that the angles of SOME add up to 360 degrees?
options: It shows that every angle of SOME is a right angle
It makes four right angles where it meets diagonal OE
It shows that the opposite angles of SOME are always supplementary
It forms two triangles whose angles make up its four angles
explanation: Correct option: (D). Diagonal SM splits SOME into triangles SEM and SOM. The six angles of these triangles add up to 180 + 180 = 360 degrees, and together they make up exactly the four angles of SOME (the angles at S and at M are each split into two parts). The angles of a general quadrilateral need not be right angles, the diagonals need not be perpendicular, and opposite angles are supplementary only in special quadrilaterals.

stem:
Assertion (A): A quadrilateral cannot have three right angles while its fourth angle is not a right angle.
Reason (R): The sum of the angles of any quadrilateral is 360 degrees.
options: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.
Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.
explanation: Correct option: (A). Both statements are true. If three angles are 90 degrees each, they add up to 270 degrees, so the fourth must be 360 - 270 = 90 degrees. The angle sum of 360 degrees is exactly what forces the fourth angle to be a right angle, so R correctly explains A. It is not just a separate true fact, which rules out option (B), and since both are true, options (C) and (D) are wrong.

OA = 6 cm and ES = 4 cm

stem: PQRS is a parallelogram, and its diagonals PR and QS are each 9 cm long. A student concludes that PQRS must be a rectangle. Which evaluation of this conclusion is correct?

Wrong, because it could also be a rhombus with equal diagonals and unequal angles

Correct, because its equal diagonals also bisect each other
explanation: Correct option: (D). The diagonals of every parallelogram bisect each other. Here they are also equal, and a quadrilateral whose diagonals are equal and bisect each other is a rectangle (the Carpenter's Problem). stem: Two congruent isosceles triangles with sides 8 cm, 8 cm and 6 cm are joined along a full common side in different ways. Which quadrilateral can NOT be obtained?
options: A rhombus with each side 8 cm
A parallelogram with sides 8 cm and 6 cm
A kite with sides 8, 8, 6 and 6 cm
A rectangle with sides 8 cm and 6 cm
explanation: Correct option: (D). Joining along the 6 cm sides as mirror images gives four 8 cm sides, a rhombus. Joining along an 8 cm side with one triangle turned round gives opposite sides 8 cm and 6 cm, a parallelogram. Joining along an 8 cm side as mirror images gives two pairs of equal adjacent sides (8, 8 and 6, 6), a kite. A rectangle is impossible: two vertices of the new figure are single angles of the triangle, and none of the triangle's angles is 90 degrees (measured, the angle between the 8 cm sides is about 44 degrees and each base angle about 68 degrees).

AO = 2 cm and angle AOB = 45 degrees
explanation: Correct option: (A). In the kite, triangles ABD and CBD are congruent (SSS), so BD bisects angle ABC; then triangles AOB and COB are congruent (SAS), so AO = OC and angle AOB = angle COB. These two angles form a linear pair, so each is 90 degrees. Hence BD is the perpendicular bisector of AC and AO = 8/2 = 4 cm. AO cannot be the whole diagonal (8 cm), and the angle at O is always 90 degrees, not 60 or 45 degrees.

stem: Using the definitions in the chapter, which one of these statements is true?
options: Every kite is also a rhombus
Every isosceles trapezium is a parallelogram
Every rhombus is also a kite
Perpendicular diagonals make a rhombus
explanation: Correct option: (C). A rhombus ABCD has all sides equal, so AB = BC and CD = DA, which meets the definition of a kite; so every rhombus is a kite. A kite with sides 6, 6, 9, 9 cm is not a rhombus, so (A) is false. An isosceles trapezium has only one pair of parallel sides, so (B) is false. A kite also has perpendicular diagonals without being a rhombus, so (D) is false.
